newsitem.title: ITALY: UN says drought is latest plague for hungry N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: UN says drought is latest plague for hungry N.Korea.

text.p: Drought in North Korea has plunged the secretive Stalinist state further towards famine after two years of severe floods devastated crops, United Nations agencies said on Monday.
In a joint statement, they said 70 percent of maize crops had been ruined by North Korea's worst drought in over half a century, compounding already grave food shortages.

On the diplomatic front, Pyongyang's normally isolationist government was preparing for landmark Korean peninsula peace talks in Washington on Tuesday which could encourage much-needed foreign investment in the impoverished state.
North Korea has been relying on international donations since unprecedented flooding in 1995-96 left thousands without food. The United Nations said on Monday the situation was now worse.

"The crop is lost. It is absolutely disastrous. It is going to be a major catastrophe that no one realised because they kept on hoping it would rain tomorrow," said Roberto Christen, an adviser with the U.N.'s Rome-based Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO).
He was part of a U.N.-coordinated mission to North Korea at the end of July to assess the drought's effects.
Official North Korean media reported over the weekend that 100mm of rain had been recorded on Saturday night, giving hope for next October's crucial harvest.
But Monday's U.N. statement said even heavy rainfall would not be enough to reverse the situation.

"The observations made so far suggest that approximately 70 percent of the country maize crop will be lost this year without any chances of recuperation even if it rains very soon," the agencies said.

The statement, issued by the U.N.'s World Food Programme (WFP) in Rome, said over 60 days without rain had destroyed 1.5 million tonnes of maize on which North Korea had been relying to feed its already hungry people.
"The drought exacerbates the fragility of the agricultural production system, already weakened by two consecutive years of losses due to flood," it said.
International aid agencies this year have stepped up calls for food aid to stave off hunger in the Stalinist state, where they warn famine is imminent, especially among young children.

In Seoul, a South Korean foreign ministry spokesman said the four-nation peace talks, which will include the two Koreas, China and the United States, could lead to large-scale food and economic assistance to the North.
The talks are aimed at bringing an official end to the 1950-53 Korean civil war that finished in an armistice and pushed Pyongyang to cut itself off from the world.
Washington and Seoul, which have pledged $52 million and $16 million respectively in response to U.N. appeals, have tied further long-term assistance to the course of the peace talks.
The WFP launched a fresh appeal last month for $46 million in food aid for North Korea on top of an earlier request for $95.5 million.
Relief workers, who recently returned from a trip to North Korea, said in Beijing on Monday that around 600,000 children aged up to five, or 38 percent of the total, were malnourished.
Tricia Parker, programme director of Oxfam Hong Kong, said thin and listless infants were a common sight in North Korea's neat and well-kept kindergartens.
"What we saw really shook all of us," Parker said. "We saw very severely malnourished children and we are quite sure that some of these children will not survive."

Also on Monday, the Swiss foreign ministry said in Berne it had received a report from a disaster expert who reported that food shortages in North Korea were getting worse, hitting especially children, women and old people.
Some reports have likened the disaster to famines seen in Ethiopia in the 1980s.
The U.N. statement said the situation could get even worse if the drought persisted and rice crops, until now less severely affected, could be jeopardised.
"The above figures are only estimates which can be significantly aggravated should the drought continue and reservoirs and other water sources further decline.
"Should the drought continue and less water be available for irrigation, the losses on paddyfields could also reach alarming proportions," it said.
